title: The instrumental: work, hobbies and company
objectives: I can form the instrumental singular of nouns, adjectives and possessives, including feminine nouns in a consonant such as 'сіль' and 'ніч'.
I can say who I am with, using 'з' and the instrumental pronouns 'мно́ю', 'тобо́ю', 'ним', 'не́ю', 'на́ми', 'ва́ми' and 'ни́ми', and say 'Taras and I' as 'ми з Тара́сом'.
I can say what someone works as, was, will be or wants to become with 'працюва́ти', 'бу́ти' and 'ста́ти', using the feminine names of professions for women.
I can talk about hobbies with 'займа́тися', 'цікави́тися', 'захо́плюватися' and 'гра́ти', and say how I do something: with a pen, by bus, in Ukrainian.
I can say where things are with 'над', 'під', 'між', 'пе́ред' and 'за', and explain why 'сіль' becomes 'сі́ллю' and 'ма́ти' becomes 'ма́тір’ю'.

vocabulary.source: to do, to take part in
vocabulary.note: The activity is in the instrumental: 'займа́тися спо́ртом', to do sports; 'займа́тися му́зикою', to study music. 'Чим ти займа́єшся?' asks what someone does, at work or in free time. Perfective 'зайня́тися', to take up.

Present 'ціка́влюся', 'ціка́вишся', 'ціка́вляться': 'л' is added after 'в', and the stress moves to 'ка'. What interests you is in the instrumental. It comes from 'ціка́вий', interesting. Perfective 'зацікави́тися', to become interested.

example.source: Sam is interested in the Ukrainian language.

vocabulary.source: to be keen on, to be passionate about
vocabulary.note: Present 'захо́плююся', 'захо́плюєшся'. What you are keen on is in the instrumental. It is a stronger word than 'цікави́тися'. Perfective 'захопи́тися', to become keen on.

example.source: My brother is passionate about soccer.

vocabulary.note: Present 'малю́ю', 'малю́єш', with '-ува-' becoming '-у-'. Perfective 'намалюва́ти'. What you draw with is in the instrumental: 'малюва́ти олівце́м'.

example.source: Oksana often paints in the park.

vocabulary.note: Present 'гра́ю', 'гра́єш'. Perfective 'зігра́ти'. A game takes 'у' or 'в' and the accusative, 'гра́ти у футбо́л'; a musical instrument takes 'на' and the locative, 'гра́ти на гіта́рі'.

example.source: The children are playing in the park.

vocabulary.note: Future 'ста́ну', 'ста́неш'; past 'став', 'ста́ла'. Imperfective partner 'става́ти' ('стаю́', 'стає́ш'). What you become is in the instrumental.

example.source: Olena became a doctor a year ago.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'спо́рту', instrumental 'спо́ртом'. The singular names sport in general.
Genitive 'футбо́лу'. The game is played with 'гра́ти у': 'гра́ти у футбо́л'.

example.target: Ми гра́ємо у футбо́л у субо́ту.
example.source: We are playing soccer on Saturday.
example.source_literal: We play in soccer on Saturday.

example.source: I love listening to Ukrainian music.

vocabulary.note: Played with 'гра́ти на' and the locative: 'гра́ти на гіта́рі'.

example.source: My father works as an engineer.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'продавця́', instrumental 'продавце́м': the 'е' drops out and the stress moves to the ending. A woman is 'продавчи́ня'.

example.source: Bohdan works as a shop assistant in a store.

vocabulary.note: With the instrumental for position: 'під столо́м', under the table.

example.source: The cat is sleeping under the table.

vocabulary.note: With the instrumental. 'Над мо́рем' and 'над о́зером' also mean by the sea and by the lake.

example.source: The sun is shining over the sea.

vocabulary.note: With the instrumental. Both things are in the instrumental, joined by 'і' or 'й': 'між ба́нком і по́штою'.

example.target: Наш дім між па́рком і шко́лою.
example.source: Our house is between the park and the school.

vocabulary.note: With the instrumental, for a place, 'пе́ред до́мом', and for a time, 'пе́ред робо́тою'.
With the instrumental for position: 'за до́мом', behind the house.

example.source: There is a park behind our house.

dialogues.title: What do you want to become?
dialogues.context: Sam and Taras sit at Andrii's café on a Saturday and talk about work and free time. They are friends and say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Се́ме, ким ти працюва́в у Кана́ді?
lines.source: Sam, what did you work as in Canada?
lines.source_literal: Sam, by-whom you worked in Canada?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я був студе́нтом, а влі́тку працюва́в офіціа́нтом.
lines.source: I was a student, and in the summer I worked as a waiter.
lines.source_literal: I was by-student, and in-summer worked by-waiter.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А ким ти хо́чеш ста́ти?
lines.source: And what do you want to become?
lines.source_literal: And by-whom you want to-become?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Журналі́стом. Я ціка́влюся Украї́ною, її́ мо́вою й му́зикою.
lines.source: A journalist. I'm interested in Ukraine, its language and its music.
lines.source_literal: By-journalist. I am-interested by-Ukraine, its by-language and by-music.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А я в шко́лі хоті́в ста́ти лі́карем. Але́ став програмі́стом.
lines.source: When I was at school, I wanted to become a doctor. But I became a programmer.
lines.source_literal: And I in school wanted to-become by-doctor. But became by-programmer.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тобі́ подо́бається твоя́ робо́та?
lines.source: Do you like your job?
lines.source_literal: To-you pleases your work?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, ду́же. А ве́чором я гра́ю на гіта́рі.
lines.source: Yes, very much. And in the evenings I play the guitar.
lines.source_literal: Yes, very. And by-evening I play on guitar.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ти гра́єш на гіта́рі? Я теж!
lines.source: You play the guitar? So do I!
lines.source_literal: You play on guitar? I too!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А спо́ртом ти займа́єшся?
lines.source: And do you do any sports?
lines.source_literal: And by-sport you do?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, у субо́ту я гра́ю у футбо́л із сусі́дом.
lines.source: Yes, on Saturdays I play soccer with my neighbor.
lines.source_literal: Yes, on Saturday I play in soccer with neighbor.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Мо́жна гра́ти з ва́ми?
lines.source: Can I play with you?
lines.source_literal: Possible to-play with you?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Звича́йно! А пі́сля футбо́лу ти зігра́єш нам на гіта́рі.
lines.source: Of course! And after the game you'll play the guitar for us.
lines.source_literal: Of-course! And after soccer you will-play to-us on guitar.

dialogues.title: Olena's colleagues
dialogues.context: Sam visits the hospital where Olena works as a doctor; the word for a hospital is 'лі́карня'. Olena introduces two people she works with. Sam says 'ти' to Olena and 'ви' to the two people he has just met.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Се́ме, приві́т! Це Мар’я́на й Ві́ктор, ми працю́ємо ра́зом.
lines.source: Hi, Sam! This is Mariana and Viktor; we work together.
lines.source_literal: Sam, hi! This Mariana and Viktor, we work together.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день! Ду́же приє́мно.
lines.source: Hello! Nice to meet you.
lines.source_literal: Good day! Very pleasant.

lines.speaker: Мар’я́на
lines.target: Ду́же приє́мно. Ви друг Оле́ни?
lines.source: Nice to meet you. Are you Olena's friend?
lines.source_literal: Very pleasant. You friend of-Olena?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так. А ви теж лі́карка?
lines.source: Yes. Are you a doctor too?
lines.source_literal: Yes. And you also doctor?

lines.speaker: Мар’я́на
lines.target: Так, я працю́ю тут лі́каркою.
lines.source: Yes, I work here as a doctor.
lines.source_literal: Yes, I work here by-doctor.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ви, Ві́кторе? Ви теж лі́кар?
lines.source: And you, Viktor? Are you a doctor too?
lines.source_literal: And you, Viktor? You also doctor?

lines.speaker: Ві́ктор
lines.target: Ні, я працю́ю тут інжене́ром. Рік тому́ я був програмі́стом.
lines.source: No, I work here as an engineer. A year ago I was a programmer.
lines.source_literal: No, I work here by-engineer. Year ago I was by-programmer.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А чому́ ви ста́ли інжене́ром?
lines.source: And why did you become an engineer?
lines.source_literal: And why you became by-engineer?

lines.speaker: Ві́ктор
lines.target: Тому́ що я ду́же ціка́влюся меди́циною.
lines.source: Because I'm very interested in medicine.
lines.source_literal: Because I very am-interested by-medicine.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А Мар’я́на захо́плюється спо́ртом. Вона́ гра́є у футбо́л!
lines.source: And Mariana is passionate about sports. She plays soccer!
lines.source_literal: And Mariana is-keen by-sport. She plays in soccer!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви гра́єте у футбо́л? Я теж!
lines.source: You play soccer? So do I!
lines.source_literal: You play in soccer? I too!

lines.speaker: Мар’я́на
lines.target: Хо́чете гра́ти з на́ми в неді́лю? Ми гра́ємо в па́рку за лі́карнею.
lines.source: Would you like to play with us on Sunday? We play in the park behind the hospital.
lines.source_literal: Want to-play with us on Sunday? We play in park behind hospital.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, ду́же хо́чу! Дя́кую.
lines.source: Yes, I'd love to! Thank you.
lines.source_literal: Yes, very want! I-thank.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А за́раз мені́ тре́ба працюва́ти. Бува́й, Се́ме!
lines.source: And now I need to work. Bye, Sam!
lines.source_literal: And now to-me necessary to-work. Bye, Sam!

dialogues.title: A concert on Friday
dialogues.context: Oksana phones Sam to invite him to a concert. Sam wants to bring his friend Mark, another Canadian in Kyiv. Oksana and Sam say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, приві́т! У п’я́тницю бу́де конце́рт украї́нської му́зики. Хо́чеш туди́ зі мно́ю?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! On Friday there's a concert of Ukrainian music. Do you want to go with me?
lines.source_literal: Sam, hi! On Friday will-be concert of-Ukrainian of-music. Want there with me?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, звича́йно! А мо́жна з дру́гом? Його́ зва́ти Марк.
lines.source: Yes, of course! Can I bring a friend? His name is Mark.
lines.source_literal: Yes, of-course! And possible with friend? Him to-call Mark.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А хто він?
lines.source: And who is he?
lines.source_literal: And who he?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Він теж кана́дець. Він працю́є в Ки́єві журналі́стом.
lines.source: He's Canadian too. He works in Kyiv as a journalist.
lines.source_literal: He also Canadian. He works in Kyiv by-journalist.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Він ціка́виться му́зикою?
lines.source: Is he interested in music?
lines.source_literal: He is-interested by-music?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же! Він гра́є на гіта́рі й малю́є.
lines.source: Very much! He plays the guitar and paints.
lines.source_literal: Very! He plays on guitar and paints.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре. Конце́рт бу́де о сьо́мій ве́чора.
lines.source: Good. The concert will be at seven in the evening.
lines.source_literal: Good. Concert will-be at seventh of-evening.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Як ми туди́ ї́демо? Авто́бусом чи метро́?
lines.source: How are we getting there? By bus or by metro?
lines.source_literal: How we there ride? By-bus or by-metro?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Метро́. Я бу́ду чека́ти вас пе́ред метро́ о пів на сьо́му.
lines.source: By metro. I'll wait for you both in front of the metro at half past six.
lines.source_literal: By-metro. I will-be to-wait you in-front-of metro at half on seventh.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А де конце́рт?
lines.source: And where is the concert?
lines.source_literal: And where concert?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У ново́му кафе́ між па́рком і музе́єм.
lines.source: In the new café between the park and the museum.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, я скажу́ Ма́ркові.
lines.source: Good, I'll tell Mark.
lines.source_literal: Good, I will-tell to-Mark.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До п’я́тниці!
lines.source: See you on Friday!
lines.source_literal: Until Friday!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Бува́й!
lines.source: Bye!

grammar.title: The instrumental case: noun endings
grammar.explanation:
The instrumental case, 'ору́дний', is named after 'ору́ддя', a tool: it is the case of the thing you do something with. It answers the questions 'ким?' (by whom? with whom?) and 'чим?' (by what? with what?), which are the instrumental forms of 'хто' and 'що'. English has no instrumental ending and uses the words 'with', 'by' and 'as' for the jobs this case does. The next notes teach those jobs one by one: company after 'з', the tool or vehicle, the role after verbs such as 'працюва́ти', the verbs of interest, and position after five prepositions.

The singular endings depend on gender and on the last letter of the noun:

- Feminine nouns in '-а' take '-ою': 'ма́ма', 'ма́мою'; 'сестра́', 'сестро́ю'.
- Feminine nouns in '-я' after a consonant take '-ею': 'ву́лиця', 'ву́лицею'; 'бабу́ся', 'бабу́сею'.
- Feminine nouns in '-а' after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ' take '-ею' as well: 'пло́ща', 'пло́щею'; 'ї́жа', 'ї́жею'.
- Feminine nouns in '-ія' take '-єю', because 'й' plus 'е' is written 'є': 'Со́фія', 'Со́фією'.
- Feminine nouns that end in a consonant take '-ю', and a single consonant before it is doubled: 'сіль', 'сі́ллю'; 'ніч', 'ні́ччю'; 'о́сінь', 'о́сінню'. After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' or 'р' an apostrophe is written instead, as in 'ма́тір’ю', the instrumental of 'ма́ти', built on the stem 'ма́тір-'. After two consonants nothing is added: 'ра́дість', joy, 'ра́дістю'.
- Masculine nouns take '-ом' after a hard consonant: 'брат', 'бра́том'; 'авто́бус', 'авто́бусом'. Masculine nouns in '-о' do the same: 'та́то', 'та́том'.
- Masculine nouns take '-ем' after a soft consonant and after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ', and '-єм' after 'й': 'вчи́тель', 'вчи́телем'; 'ключ', 'ключе́м'; 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́єм'.
- Neuter nouns take '-ом' after a hard consonant and '-ем' when they end in '-е': 'мі́сто', 'мі́стом'; 'мо́ре', 'мо́рем'. Neuter nouns in '-я' after a doubled consonant take '-ям': 'життя́', 'життя́м'.

Two groups need care. 'Лі́кар' ends in 'р' but belongs to the soft group, as its genitive 'лі́каря' shows, so its instrumental is 'лі́карем'. A masculine noun in '-а' that names a man, such as 'Мико́ла', declines like 'ма́ма', so its instrumental is 'Мико́лою'; it stays masculine for agreement. Nouns that never change, such as 'кафе́', 'метро́' and 'меню́', keep their form in the instrumental too.

The stress of the instrumental is usually the stress of the genitive singular: 'сестри́', 'сестро́ю'; 'стола́', 'столо́м'; 'ключа́', 'ключе́м'. 'Ма́ти' builds its instrumental on the stem 'ма́тір-', with 'і' where the genitive 'ма́тері' has 'е', so learn 'ма́тір’ю' as it is. The note on spelling and sound explains the doubled letters and the apostrophe.

examples.target: Оле́на була́ у Льво́ві з ма́тір’ю.
examples.source: Olena was in Lviv with her mother.
Sam is talking with Andrii.
I went for a walk with Grandma.

examples.target: Ми були́ в кафе́ з Со́фією.
examples.source: We were at the café with Sofiia.
The children went for a walk with Dad.

grammar.title: Adjectives, possessives and pronouns in the instrumental
grammar.explanation:
An adjective, a possessive pronoun or a demonstrative pronoun before a noun in the instrumental takes the instrumental too. There are two endings in the singular:

- '-им' for masculine and neuter: 'з нови́м дру́гом', 'під вели́ким столо́м', 'з на́шим бра́том'
- '-ою' for feminine, the same ending as the noun: 'з ново́ю по́другою', 'з на́шою ма́мою'

Soft-stem adjectives write '-ім' and '-ьою': 'си́ній', 'си́нім', 'си́ньою'. 'Мій' and 'твій' become 'мої́м' and 'твої́м' in the masculine and neuter, and 'моє́ю' and 'твоє́ю' in the feminine. 'Цей' and 'той' become 'цим' and 'тим'; 'ця' and 'та' become 'ціє́ю' and 'тіє́ю'. 'Його́', 'її́' and 'їх' meaning his, her and their never change, because they are genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́': 'з її́ бра́том', with her brother.

The personal pronouns have their own instrumental forms, listed in the table. The forms for 'він', 'воно́', 'вона́' and 'вони́' all begin with 'н': 'ним', 'не́ю', 'ни́ми', and 'ним' serves both 'він' and 'воно́'. Before 'мно́ю' the preposition 'з' takes the form 'зі', by the euphony rule of the unit on stress: 'зі мно́ю', with me. Before the other pronouns it is 'з', or 'із' between consonants: 'з тобо́ю', 'Тара́с із ни́ми'.

'З ким?' asks 'with whom?': 'З ким ти був у кіно́?' (Who were you at the movies with?) The answer has the instrumental: 'З Тара́сом.' or 'З ним.'

examples.source: Did you have coffee with him?
I talked with her yesterday.

examples.target: Окса́на гуля́ла з на́шою ново́ю сусі́дкою.
examples.source: Oksana went for a walk with our new neighbor.

examples.target: Сем був у музе́ї з мої́м бра́том.
examples.source: Sam was at the museum with my brother.

examples.target: З ким ти був у кіно́?
examples.source: Who were you at the movies with?
examples.source_literal: With whom you were in cinema?

grammar.title: Company, means and adverbs of time
grammar.explanation:
The preposition 'з' has two meanings, and the case after it tells them apart. With the genitive it means 'from': 'з Ки́єва', from Kyiv. With the instrumental it means 'with', in the sense of together with: 'з дру́гом', with a friend; 'з Окса́ною', with Oksana. 'З', 'із' and 'зі' follow the same euphony rules in both meanings.

Ukrainian often says 'Taras and I' with 'ми' and 'з'. 'Ми з Тара́сом' is literally 'we with Taras' and means 'Taras and I'. The verb is plural, because 'ми' is the subject: 'Ми з Тара́сом працю́ємо ра́зом.' (Taras and I work together.) In the same way 'ми з тобо́ю' means 'you and I'.

The same 'з' names what comes with a thing, which explains phrases you have used since the first units:

- 'ка́ва з молоко́м', coffee with milk: 'молоко́' takes '-ом', as 'мі́сто' does.
- 'чай із цу́кром', tea with sugar: 'цу́кор' loses its 'о' before the ending, as in the genitive 'цу́кру'.
- 'З днем наро́дження!', happy birthday, literally 'with day of-birth': 'день' loses its 'е', as in 'дня'. It is short for 'Віта́ю з днем наро́дження!', where 'віта́ю' means 'I congratulate'.

The instrumental alone, with no preposition, names the means: the tool you use or the vehicle you travel by. English says 'with' or 'by':

- 'писа́ти ру́чкою', to write with a pen; 'малюва́ти олівце́м', to draw with a pencil
- 'ї́хати авто́бусом', to go by bus; 'ї́хати метро́', to go by metro, where 'метро́' does not change

A tool takes no 'з': 'з ру́чкою' means having a pen with you, not writing with it. 'Ї́хати авто́бусом' and 'ї́хати на авто́бусі', from the unit on directions, mean the same, and both are common.

A language is a means too, of speaking or writing. 'Говори́ти украї́нською мо́вою' is literally 'to-speak by-Ukrainian by-language': 'мо́вою' is the instrumental of 'мо́ва', and the adjective agrees with it in the feminine instrumental. In speech 'мо́вою' is usually left out, which gives the form you met in the unit on the present tense: 'Я говорю́ украї́нською.' So 'украї́нською' is a form of an adjective, not an adverb. Ukrainian also has an adverb with the same meaning, 'по-украї́нськи', in Ukrainian, written with a hyphen after 'по'. It is common after 'говори́ти' and 'розумі́ти' and in the question 'Як це по-украї́нськи?' (How do you say this in Ukrainian?). Other languages work the same way: 'англі́йською', 'по-англі́йськи'.

Some words for a part of the day or a season have an instrumental form that has become an adverb of time. Each adverb is spelled and stressed like the instrumental of its noun:

- 'ра́нком', in the morning, and 'ве́чором', in the evening
- 'ні́ччю', at night
- 'зимо́ю', 'весно́ю', 'лі́том', 'о́сінню', in winter, in spring, in summer, in autumn

They mean the same as the adverbs 'вра́нці', 'уве́чері', 'вночі́', 'взи́мку', 'навесні́', 'влі́тку' and 'восени́'.

rows: I'm going for a walk with my brother.
It is cold here in winter.

examples.target: Ми з Окса́ною були́ в кіно́.
examples.source: Oksana and I were at the movies.
examples.source_literal: We with Oksana were in cinema.

examples.source: Oksana is going to the library by metro.
I write in pencil.
How do you say this in Ukrainian?
Happy birthday, Taras!
In summer we vacation at the sea.

grammar.title: Work and roles: 'працюва́ти', 'бу́ти' and 'ста́ти'
grammar.explanation:
In the present tense Ukrainian has no word for 'is', and a profession after a pronoun stays in the nominative: 'Він інжене́р.' (He is an engineer.) 'Я студе́нтка.' (I am a student.)

When a verb links the person to the role, the role goes into the instrumental:

- 'працюва́ти', to work as: 'Він працю́є інжене́ром.' (He works as an engineer, literally 'he works by-engineer')
- 'бу́ти' in the past and the future: 'Він був студе́нтом.' (He was a student); 'Я бу́ду вчи́телькою.' (I will be a teacher)
- 'ста́ти', to become: 'Я хо́чу ста́ти лі́карем.' (I want to become a doctor)

The question is 'ким?', because the answer names a person. 'Ким ти працю́єш?', literally 'by-whom you work?', means 'What do you do for a living?', and 'Ким ти хо́чеш ста́ти?' means 'What do you want to become?'.

'Ста́ти' is perfective: 'ста́ну', 'ста́неш' is its future and 'став', 'ста́ла' its past. Its imperfective partner 'става́ти' ('стаю́', 'стає́ш') names becoming as a process or as something that happens again and again.

The role names the person, so a woman's profession is a feminine noun with feminine endings. Most feminine names of professions add '-ка' to the masculine noun, as 'студе́нтка', 'лі́карка' and 'вчи́телька' do:

- 'інжене́р', 'інжене́рка'
- 'програмі́ст', 'програмі́стка'
- 'журналі́ст', 'журналі́стка'

'Продаве́ць', a shop assistant, takes the suffix '-иня' instead: it loses its 'е', and its 'ц' changes to 'ч' before the suffix, which gives 'продавчи́ня'. In the instrumental the nouns in '-ка' take '-ою' ('інжене́ркою'), and 'продавчи́ня' takes '-ею' ('продавчи́нею'), by the rules of the first note.

With 'ви' said to one person, the verb is plural but the role is singular: 'Ви були́ вчи́телькою?' (Were you a teacher?)

examples.source: What do you do for a living?
My mom works as a teacher.
My grandfather was an engineer.
I will be a journalist.
Sofiia became a programmer.

grammar.title: Hobbies: verbs with the instrumental, and 'гра́ти'
grammar.explanation:
Three reflexive verbs about interests and free time take the instrumental. English uses a preposition with them ('interested in', 'keen on') or a direct object ('to do sports'); Ukrainian uses the case alone:

- 'займа́тися', to do, to take part in: 'займа́тися спо́ртом', to do sports; 'займа́тися му́зикою', to study music
- 'цікави́тися', to be interested in: 'цікави́тися футбо́лом'
- 'захо́плюватися', to be keen on, a stronger word: 'захо́плюватися му́зикою'

The '-ся' is part of each verb, as in 'прокида́тися'. The question is 'чим?'. 'Чим ти займа́єшся?' (What do you do?) can ask about work as well as about free time, and 'Чим ти ціка́вишся?' asks what interests someone.

Three ways of talking about music show three cases:

- 'Я люблю́ му́зику.' (I love music): the person is the subject, and the music is the direct object, in the accusative.
- 'Мені́ подо́бається му́зика.' (I like music, literally 'to-me pleases music'): the music is the subject, and the person is in the dative.
- 'Я ціка́влюся му́зикою.' (I am interested in music): the person is the subject, and the music is in the instrumental.

'Цікави́тися' adds 'л' in the 'я' and 'вони́' forms, as 'люби́ти' does, and its present has the stress on 'ка'; the table gives its forms. In 'захо́плюватися' the '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працюва́ти': 'захо́плююся', 'захо́плюєшся', 'захо́плюються'.

'Гра́ти', to play, takes no instrumental. A game takes 'у' or 'в' and the accusative: 'гра́ти у футбо́л'. A musical instrument takes 'на' and the locative: 'гра́ти на гіта́рі', 'гра́ти на піа́ніно', on the piano, a noun that never changes. So 'Тара́с гра́є у футбо́л.' is about a sport, and 'Тара́с гра́є на гіта́рі.' is about music.

examples.source: What do you do?
Taras is interested in soccer.
Olena and I do sports.
Oksana is passionate about music.

examples.target: Тара́с гра́є на гіта́рі, а Сем гра́є у футбо́л.
examples.source: Taras plays the guitar, and Sam plays soccer.
examples.source_literal: Taras plays on guitar, and Sam plays in soccer.

grammar.title: Where things are: 'над', 'під', 'між', 'пе́ред' and 'за'
grammar.explanation:
Five prepositions say where something is in relation to something else, and they take the instrumental. They answer 'де?', as 'у' and 'на' with the locative do:

- 'над', above, over: 'над столо́м', above the table
- 'під', under: 'під столо́м', under the table
- 'пе́ред', in front of: 'пе́ред до́мом', in front of the house
- 'за', behind: 'за до́мом', behind the house
- 'між', between: 'між ба́нком і по́штою', between the bank and the post office

After 'між' both nouns are in the instrumental, joined by 'і' or 'й'. 'Стіл' and 'дім' show the 'о' of their other forms, because the ending opens the syllable: 'столо́м', 'до́мом'.

'Пе́ред' also works in time, meaning 'before': 'пе́ред робо́тою', before work; 'пе́ред конце́ртом', before the concert. Its opposite 'пі́сля', after, takes the genitive: 'пі́сля робо́ти'.

Some of these phrases have a meaning of their own. 'Над мо́рем' and 'над о́зером' mean by the sea and by the lake, on the shore, as in 'відпочива́ти над мо́рем', to vacation by the sea. 'Сиді́ти за столо́м' means to sit at the table, for a meal or for work.

A pronoun after these prepositions takes its instrumental form: 'за ним', behind him; 'пе́ред на́ми', in front of us; 'між на́ми', between us.

rows: The sun is shining over the city.
The cat is under the table.
The bus is in front of the house.
The bank is behind the post office.
The school is between the park and the pharmacy.

examples.target: Пе́ред конце́ртом ми були́ в кафе́.
examples.source: Before the concert we were at the café.
examples.source_literal: Before concert we were in café.

examples.source: We had a vacation by the sea.

examples.target: Ми сиді́ли за столо́м і говори́ли.
examples.source: We sat at the table and talked.
examples.source_literal: We sat behind table and talked.

examples.source: The store is between the pharmacy and the bank.
The bus is waiting in front of the school.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: сі́ллю, ні́ччю, ма́тір’ю and зі мно́ю
grammar.explanation:
Every new word and form in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones the instrumental brings up.

A feminine noun that ends in one consonant after a vowel doubles that consonant before the ending '-ю': 'сіль', 'сі́ллю' [ˈsʲilʲːu]; 'ніч', 'ні́ччю' [ˈnʲit͡ʃːu]; 'о́сінь', 'о́сінню' [ˈɔsʲinʲːu]; 'по́дорож', 'по́дорожжю'. The ending once began with the sound [j], which merged with the consonant before it and made it long, the same change that gave 'життя́'. As in 'життя́', two letters write one long consonant. A soft consonant stays soft, so 'сі́ллю' has a long soft [lʲː]; 'ч' and 'ж' are never soft, so 'ні́ччю' has a long hard [t͡ʃː]. The soft sign of 'сіль' and 'о́сінь' is not written before '-ю', because 'ю' itself shows that the consonant is soft.

The consonants 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' and 'р' do not merge with [j] this way. After them the [j] stays a separate sound, and the apostrophe shows it, as in 'м’я́со': 'ма́ти' has the instrumental 'ма́тір’ю' [ˈmɑtʲirju], with a soft 'т' before 'і' and a hard 'р'. After two consonants nothing is doubled: 'ра́дість', 'ра́дістю'.

'Зі мно́ю' follows the euphony rule for 'з': before the cluster 'мн' it becomes 'зі', so that three consonants do not meet. 'Мно́ю' has two syllables, [ˈmnɔju], with 'м' and 'н' said together at the start. Elsewhere the rules for 'з', 'із' and 'зі' work as before: 'з ма́мою', 'Тара́с із Се́мом', 'чай із цу́кром'.

The other new words:

- 'Ціка́влюся' adds 'л' after 'в' in the 'я' and 'вони́' forms, as 'люблю́' does, and moves the stress from 'ви' to 'ка'.
- 'Займа́ється' and 'захо́плюється' end in '-ться', said [t͡sʲːɑ]; 'займа́єшся' ends in '-шся', said [sʲːɑ].
- 'Захо́плююся' has 'ю' twice: the first softens the 'л' before it, and the second, after a vowel, is said [ju].
- 'Продаве́ць' loses its 'е' when an ending is added, as 'оліве́ць' does: 'продавця́', 'продавце́м', 'олівце́м'. The 'ць' is soft at the end of the word and before 'я'.
- In 'продавчи́ня' the 'ц' of 'продаве́ць' becomes 'ч' before the suffix '-иня'.
- 'Стіл', 'дім' and 'ве́чір' show 'о' in an open syllable: 'столо́м', 'до́мом', 'ве́чором'. 'День', 'цу́кор' and 'ра́нок' drop their 'е' and 'о': 'днем', 'цу́кром', 'ра́нком'.
- 'По-украї́нськи' is one word written with a hyphen. Its 'по' has one syllable and no stress mark, and the soft sign makes the 'с' soft before 'к'.
- 'Між' ends in a voiced 'ж', and 'під', 'над' and 'пе́ред' in a voiced 'д'; they stay voiced at the end of the word, as 'хліб' does.
- 'Гіта́ра' begins with the voiced [ɦ] of 'г'.
- 'Інжене́р' [inʒɛˈnɛr] has a hard 'ж' and a hard 'н' before 'е', and its unstressed first 'е' leans toward 'и'.
- 'Журналі́ст' has a soft 'л' before 'і'.

examples.source: Taras is eating bread with salt.
Olena is sitting with me.
Are you interested in music?
Sam is talking with the shop assistant.
At night the children sleep.

culture.title: Names for women's professions
culture.text:
Ukrainian names a woman's profession with a feminine noun, and it has long done so. The most common suffixes are:

- '-ка': 'вчи́телька', 'лі́карка', 'студе́нтка', 'журналі́стка'
- '-иня': 'продавчи́ня', 'господи́ня', the woman who runs a home
- '-иця': 'учени́ця', a schoolgirl

The official rules of Ukrainian spelling adopted in 2019 list these suffixes for forming feminine nouns. Forms such as 'інжене́рка', 'програмі́стка', 'авто́рка' (author) and 'дире́кторка' (director) are now widely used in newspapers, on television, at universities and in job advertisements. Some speakers, mostly older ones, still name a woman's profession with the masculine noun, especially in official titles. This course uses the feminine noun for every woman.

At a first meeting Ukrainians often ask about work: 'Ким ви працю́єте?' to someone they call 'ви', and 'Ким ти працю́єш?' to a friend. The answer usually names the place as well: 'Я працю́ю вчи́телькою в шко́лі.' (I work as a teacher at a school.) The question 'Чим ти займа́єшся?' can mean either 'What do you do for a living?' or 'What do you do in your free time?', and the answer shows which one the speaker heard.

exercises.prompt: Match each profession with its English name
Match each preposition with its meaning
Match each phrase with its meaning

pairs.source: with you, said to a friend

choices: The cat is sitting under the window.
The cat is sitting under the table.
The cat is sitting in front of the window.

exercises.prompt: Which questions does the instrumental case answer?
exercises.explanation: 'Ким?' and 'чим?' are the instrumental forms of 'хто' and 'що'. 'Кого́? чого́?' ask for the genitive, and 'кому́? чому́?' for the dative.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'ма́ма' is the instrumental?
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns in '-а' take '-ою' in the instrumental. 'Ма́мі' is the dative or the locative, and 'ма́му' is the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'брат' is the instrumental?
exercises.explanation: Masculine nouns with a hard stem take '-ом'. 'Бра́тові' is the dative, and 'бра́та' is the genitive and the accusative.

exercises.hint_source: I am going for a walk with my sister.
exercises.explanation: 'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental. 'Сестра́' takes '-ою', with the stress on the ending, as in the genitive 'сестри́'.

exercises.hint_source: Sam lives with a male friend in Kyiv.
exercises.explanation: Company takes 'з' and the instrumental. 'Друг' has a hard stem, so it takes '-ом'.

choices: I want to become a doctor.
I want to become a journalist.

exercises.prompt: Why is the instrumental of 'вчи́тель' 'вчи́телем', with '-ем'?
choices: Its stem ends in a soft consonant, and soft stems take '-ем'.
exercises.explanation: The soft sign shows that 'л' is soft, and masculine nouns with a soft stem take '-ем'. Hard stems take '-ом', as in 'бра́том'.
The instrumental of 'я' is 'мно́ю', and before it 'з' takes the form 'зі'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'з' take the form 'зі' in 'зі мно́ю'?
choices: 'Зі' is the form of 'з' that takes the genitive.
Before the cluster 'мн', 'з' becomes 'зі' for euphony.
exercises.explanation: The euphony rule keeps three consonants from meeting, so 'з' becomes 'зі' before 'мн'. Before the other pronouns it is 'з', or 'із' between consonants: 'з тобо́ю', 'Тара́с із ним'.

exercises.prompt_target: Ми з ___ ча́сто гра́ємо у футбо́л.
exercises.hint_source: He and I often play soccer.
exercises.explanation: 'Ми з' plus the instrumental means 'X and I'. The instrumental of 'він' is 'ним'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Ми з Оле́ною п’ємо́ ка́ву.' mean?
choices: Olena and I are drinking coffee.
We are drinking coffee from Olena.
exercises.explanation: 'Ми з Оле́ною' is literally 'we with Olena' and means 'Olena and I'. The verb is plural because 'ми' is the subject.

exercises.hint_source: My uncle works as an engineer.
exercises.explanation: After 'працюва́ти' the role is in the instrumental: 'інжене́р' takes '-ом'.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana wants to become a journalist.
exercises.explanation: 'Ста́ти' takes the instrumental. Oksana is a woman, so the feminine noun 'журналі́стка' is used, and it takes '-ою'.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes 'Рік тому́ він був ___.' (A year ago he was a student.)?
exercises.explanation: In the past and the future, 'бу́ти' takes the role in the instrumental: 'Він був студе́нтом.' In the present there is no verb, and the nominative is used: 'Він студе́нт.'

exercises.prompt: What does the question 'Ким ти працю́єш?' ask?
choices: What you do for a living
exercises.explanation: 'Ким' is the instrumental of 'хто', the role after 'працюва́ти': literally 'by-whom you work?'. 'With whom' would be 'з ким', and 'where' would be 'де'.

exercises.hint_source: Mykola works as a shop assistant in a store.
exercises.explanation: The role after 'працюва́ти' is in the instrumental. 'Продаве́ць' drops its 'е' and takes '-ем' after the soft 'ц', with the stress on the ending.
The tool is in the instrumental with no preposition: 'ру́чка' becomes 'ру́чкою'.

exercises.prompt: Why is there no 'з' in 'Я малю́ю олівце́м.'?
choices: 'Олівце́м' is the genitive, which needs no preposition.
A tool is in the instrumental alone; 'з олівце́м' means having a pencil with you.
exercises.explanation: The instrumental alone names the means. 'З' with the instrumental means together with, so 'з олівце́м' says that the pencil is with you, not that you draw with it.

choices: We're going to the market by metro.

exercises.explanation: 'Цікави́тися' takes the instrumental: 'му́зика' becomes 'му́зикою'.
'Займа́тися' takes the activity in the instrumental: 'спорт' becomes 'спо́ртом'.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Окса́на гра́є ___ футбо́л.'?
exercises.explanation: A game takes 'у' or 'в' and the accusative: 'гра́ти у футбо́л'. 'На' with the locative is for musical instruments.
A musical instrument takes 'на' and the locative, not the instrumental: 'на гіта́рі'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I am interested in soccer'?
exercises.explanation: 'Цікави́тися' takes the instrumental, 'футбо́лом'. 'Мені́ подо́бається футбо́л.' means 'I like soccer', and 'Я гра́ю у футбо́л.' means 'I play soccer'.

exercises.hint_source: The pharmacy is between the bank and the post office.
exercises.explanation: After 'між' both nouns are in the instrumental: 'по́шта' becomes 'по́штою'.

exercises.hint_source: Your key is under the book.
exercises.explanation: 'Під' takes the instrumental for position: 'кни́га' becomes 'кни́гою'.

exercises.hint_source: The park is behind the school.
exercises.explanation: 'За' meaning behind takes the instrumental: 'шко́ла' becomes 'шко́лою'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'над о́зером' mean in 'Ми бу́демо відпочива́ти над о́зером.'?
exercises.explanation: 'Над' means above, and 'над о́зером' and 'над мо́рем' mean by the lake and by the sea, on the shore.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'сіль' become 'сі́ллю' in the instrumental?
choices: Before '-ю' a single final consonant is doubled, and the two letters write one long sound.
The 'л' is doubled in every form of 'сіль'.
exercises.explanation: In feminine nouns in a consonant the ending '-ю' once began with [j], which merged with the consonant and made it long. The genitive is 'со́лі', with one 'л'.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the instrumental of 'ма́ти', mother?
exercises.explanation: The instrumental is built on 'ма́тір-' with '-ю', and after 'р' an apostrophe is written instead of a doubled letter. 'Ма́тері' is the genitive, the dative and the locative, and 'ма́тір' is the accusative.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я говорю́ украї́нською.', what is 'украї́нською'?
choices: The instrumental of 'украї́нська мо́ва', with 'мо́вою' left out
An adverb meaning 'in a Ukrainian way'
exercises.explanation: 'Говори́ти украї́нською мо́вою' is literally 'to-speak by-Ukrainian by-language', and 'мо́вою' is usually left out. The adverb with the same meaning is 'по-украї́нськи'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what does Sam want to become?
exercises.explanation: Sam answers 'Журналі́стом.' Taras wanted to become a doctor at school but became a programmer.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what does Viktor work as?
exercises.explanation: Viktor says 'я працю́ю тут інжене́ром'. A year ago he was a programmer, and Mariana is the doctor.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, how will Oksana, Sam and Mark get to the concert?
exercises.explanation: Sam asks 'Авто́бусом чи метро́?', and Oksana answers 'Метро́.' She will wait for them in front of the metro.

exercises.prompt_source: The café is between the park and the museum.
Sam is going to the university by bus.
My sister works as a teacher.
exercises.explanation: After 'працюва́ти' the role is in the instrumental, and a woman's profession is the feminine noun 'вчи́телька'.

exercises.prompt_source: I want to become a doctor.
exercises.explanation: 'Ста́ти' takes the instrumental: 'лі́карем' for a man, 'лі́каркою' for a woman.

exercises.prompt_source: Taras and I play the guitar.
answers: Ми з Тара́сом гра́ємо на гіта́рі.
Тара́с і я гра́ємо на гіта́рі.
Я й Тара́с гра́ємо на гіта́рі.
exercises.explanation: 'Ми з Тара́сом' is the usual way to say 'Taras and I'. An instrument takes 'на' and the locative.
The vehicle is in the instrumental, 'авто́бусом', or takes 'на' and the locative, 'на авто́бусі'.
